summary.prose: The daemon's store failed, and the daemon then could not be stopped, because another process that had the live store open closed it and removed the store's locks. This Story makes the store refuse the live path to every process but the daemon, and gives the two tests that reached the live store a temporary one. The MCP server's process also opens the live store today, for every analyze step and not only for its cache; that use is removed by Story s11, so until s11 lands the MCP server is let in by an explicit, temporary allowance, and the refusal is complete only once s11 has removed it. A store failure is recorded once with its true cause and shown in the daemon's status, and a stop always ends: the daemon ends itself at once when it knows its store has failed, and the control script and the CLI's stop force the end when a stop overruns.

hldContextSlice.frameworkSummary: Three layers, each depending only on the one below. Layer 1, the file commit: the store has one write operation for a file, which in a single LMDB transaction replaces the file's entities, replaces its relationships and its pending relationships, and advances the repository's generation and completeness counters. It grows out of the existing whole-file replacement (reindexFile), which already replaces a file's entities in one transaction but removes relationships only for entities that disappeared from the file; the commit goes further and replaces the outgoing relationships of every entity of the file. The indexer's refresh, the delete event and the repair all call it; a file is selected for it by one filter built from the repository's ignore files. A relationship is never dropped in the commit: when its target is not stored it becomes a pending row, and pending rows are completed only by the passes that own them: the cross-file pass for code symbols, and the two endpoint passes of the external-services Epic for theirs. Layer 2, the recorded state: one row per repository holds the generation and what is known to be incomplete (relationships awaiting a target that is in an indexed repository, relationships that could not be written, entities without vectors). The four repository status values keep their meaning; completeness is a separate field read from this row and shown wherever status is shown, so a repository with anything outstanding does not read as fully ready. Layer 3, derived data: evidence is a one-byte value on the relationship row, written in the commit, by the cross-file pass and by every other writer of a stored relationship; subsystem grouping, subsystem summaries and model-proposed document relationships are queued passes that start only from a repository whose state is complete, write their own tables, and stamp what they wrote with the generation it was computed from. All new stored data arrives as steps on the existing migration chain (SCHEMA_VERSION 4 onward); no existing edge key or kind byte changes.

boundary.internal: The cause, which ISSUE-0d577569 records as not known, was reproduced on 2026-10-11 and is not the system's semaphore limit, which the library's message names, but the loss of the daemon's own file lock on the store's lock file, after which another process that opens and closes the store removes the store's semaphores; the daemon's next write then fails with the library's message about the limit, and its exit hangs in the library's close. What in the daemon closes a second descriptor on the lock file is not yet identified. First, therefore, the remedy that does not depend on finding it: the live store is opened by the daemon alone, and any other process is refused it. Second, a bound on the whole shutdown including the store's close, so that a close that hangs ends in an exit. Third, recording a store failure of this kind and stating it in the daemon's status. None of this is consumed by another Story.

adjacentBoundaries.internal: The rule that a relationship with an absent target becomes pending instead of being skipped, at each of the six places in src/db/relations.ts where one is lost today (the resolved write's skip on a missing endpoint and its skip on a kind with no byte, promoteToResolved, promoteResolvedBatch, and the pending write's discard of a row without its file or repository and of a row whose repository is not registered), each either kept as pending or counted as unwritable with a reason; the set of files whose parse or commit failed in a full index, persisted with their paths until they next commit; which fields of the state are recounted on open and which are persisted and carried over; the classification of a pending relationship as awaiting-target, ambiguous or no-candidate, with the external-service rows classed apart and the two endpoint passes counted in when a full index is finished; the class is stored on the pending row itself, in its existing free-form record, so no stored form changes, a row the cross-file pass has not yet attempted counts as awaiting-target, and the recount on open reads the stored class and does not run resolution again; the extension of the cross-file pass to complete relationships awaiting a target by id, for imports and the other code-symbol kinds as well as calls and inheritance, and to follow a re-exporting file to the function it re-exports; the lookup of pending rows by the id they await, with its migration step, and the pass after a file event visiting the rows that await an entity of the files just committed; the change of the reindex request so that it deletes the repository's rows in the graph store and the vector store and builds them again from every file, in place of today's skip of unchanged files, with no separate repair request, returning to pending the relationships that other repositories hold into the deleted entities, and its queuing by the migration for every repository indexed before this change, which starts as not complete; the storing of the repository entity so that the manifest step's dependency relationships are written; the measurement on this repository, before and after a repair, of the awaiting-target, ambiguous, no-candidate and unwritable counts, with unwritable expected to be zero; the IndexState row, its migration step, its recount on open, and the derivation of repository status from it, as a completeness field returned beside the unchanged status by the daemon's status and stats requests and shown in the CLI's repository pane and in both editor plugins; and the analyzer's read of it: an analyzer lookup that reads relationships of a repository that is not complete says so in its result, with the counts, so that an answer over an incomplete graph is not returned as a plain fact. The choice, in this Story's design, of the function reached only through a re-exporting file that the repair is measured on, since the issue's own example (pickScope) has been removed from the source. Raising the log level of a refused relationship from debug is internal. Until Story s2 lands, s1 applies its rule inside the existing separate writes.

The extension of the existing whole-file replacement into the file commit (relationships and pending rows in the same transaction as entities; outgoing relationships of surviving entities replaced, not only those of entities that disappeared; incoming relationships of a removed entity returned to pending), the move of the indexer's refresh and delete paths and of the clean-up pass's removal of a stored file onto it, and the retirement of the separate delete-then-upsert sequence in the indexer. The handling of vectors after the commit: writing the entity row with its embedding marker empty and setting it in a second transaction only after the vector write succeeds, counting an entity with an empty marker in IndexState, comparing entity ids with the vector table on open in both directions, so that a vector left behind by a failed removal is deleted before a plain insert can meet it, and the extension of the existing reembed job to run on daemon start and after an index, with a vector write for an entity whose marker is empty made an upsert, except for an entity first allocated in the same commit, which keeps the plain insert. Three things in that job change with it: it applies the embed step's own selection instead of forcing every entity, so empty-body entities (external endpoints, module stubs) stay unselected and uncounted; its update of an embedding writes the vector first and sets the marker in a second transaction, where today it sets the marker first; and the marker carries the model of the backend that is active, not one fixed name. Which entities count as unembedded (those the embed step selects) and the separate recorded reason when the embedding backend is unavailable. The count of a file whose commit fails on a file event. The queue rule that index jobs go ahead of other jobs and that a long job yields between its units, so that a commit is not held behind a model pass. How a reader sees the old or the new set during a commit is the store's ordinary transaction isolation and needs no new mechanism.

The by-file and by-repository index of entity rows, its migration step that builds it for an existing store, and its upkeep. No single entity-row write exists today: there are seven raw put and remove sites across src/db/entities.ts and src/db/graph/migrations.ts, and the existing name index is kept in step by a helper each site must remember to call. This Story introduces one put and one remove function for entity rows that maintain the name index and the new index together, routes every raw site through them, and adds a test that fails when a raw put or remove appears outside them. Upkeep therefore sits beneath every caller, so that neither today's writers nor the file commit need to know of it and this Story does not depend on s2. The two reads (findEntitiesByFile, listEntitiesForRepo) keep their results and their callers; a new existence check answers whether a repository holds any entity, and the analyzer's scope check uses it.

The refusal, with a named error and its own code, of a search or analyze request about a repository whose status is indexing, at the analyzer's scope check and at the daemon's search requests, carrying the status and how far the run has got (files done of files selected, and when it began), read from the indexer's running job; the tools that rest on the analyzer (the workflow steps, triage, code review) pass that error on as it is. The order of the analyzer's run: the refusal of a scope the index does not hold comes before a size is announced, or the announcement says the size could not be counted. The named cause and error code for a failed read of the last-indexed time and for a failed lookup, and the three other defects of ISSUE-e2bcadd9 (the wrong provider named, the scope resolved before the cache, and failure text matched inside echoed output). This Story does not read IndexState: it works with the checks the analyzer has today, so that it stays independent of s1.

The in-process matcher of the gitignore grammar over nested ignore files and its conformance test against git; the move onto the one filter of every site that reads the list today in src/indexer/index.ts (the full walk, the start-up scan for changed files, the file event, the clean-up pass, and the two places that seed the list when a repository is registered), of the watcher, and of the analyzer's reader, its two exploration walkers and its infra walker (src/analyze/runtimes/infra/_shared.ts), each of which has its own list of names today, and of the indexer's source-root detection (src/indexer/source-roots.ts), whose own list would otherwise hide a package in a directory the filter includes; a search of the source for such lists found five more, in the daemon's four file-search tools (glob, grep, list-dir, recent under src/daemon/tools/builtins/search) and in the review probe (src/workflow/review/probe.ts), which search the working tree as text, do not decide what the index holds, and are deliberately left as they are; the filter keeps answering for a directory that holds an included file, as the analyzer's reader does now; the retirement of the bare-name list and of the ignore entry in the repository's .insrc config; the two built-in exclusions (generated or minified files, the .insrc directory) applied inside the filter so that the full walk and the file event no longer differ on them; the handling of a change to an ignore file as an event that removes and adds files, and the comparison by content hash of the clone's exclude file and the global ignore file, which the watcher cannot see, whenever the filter is used; the queued step that proposes a root ignore file with the cheap-tier model when a repository is added without one, its fallback, and the rule that an existing file is never written. Two points were decided by the stakeholder: the filter honours all three of git's ignore sources (the .gitignore files, the clone's exclude file, the user's global ignore file), and a file git tracks is indexed even when a rule matches it, so the filter takes git's list of tracked files as an input and a plain folder is filtered by the rules alone.

The one-byte encoding of evidence as the value of a relationship row; the points in the per-file resolver and the cross-file pass that decide 'extracted' or 'inferred' ('chosen' is reserved and not written, since an ambiguous relationship stays pending with its candidates); the passing of evidence as an argument to the store's resolved write and promote operations, so that the two endpoint passes write 'inferred' and the manifest step writes 'extracted' and no relationship written after this change reads 'unknown'; the carrying of evidence through the store's traversal reads and the daemon's caller and callee requests; the marking of inferred and chosen relationships in the analyzer's lookups and answers. No migration rewrites existing rows, since an empty value reads as 'unknown'.

The grouping of a complete repository's code entities into subsystems, its determinism, the tables for membership, connections and summaries and their migration step; the queued pass and its trigger on a new generation; the cheap-tier summary of a subsystem whose membership changed; the daemon request that returns subsystems; the addition of subsystem context to the analyzer's context builder; the statement that groups rest on an incomplete or older graph. Which relationships count toward grouping, and with what weight by evidence, is decided here.

One reader per added language (Rust, C#, C, C++) in the existing parser registry with a guarded load, as the Kotlin reader has; the structured reading of SQL in place of the whole-file document, keeping the document entity for retrieval; any entity kinds this needs, appended to the fixed byte table without renumbering; the additions to the Language union; the daemon request that lists the languages read and why any was skipped. Each language can be delivered on its own.

The reading of links and references between documents, and from a document to code, as relationships of the existing REFERENCES kind written in the file commit with evidence 'extracted'; the queued mid-tier pass over new or changed documents and its own table of model-proposed relationships; the hand-checked set, the measurement, and the recorded figures that switch the capability on or leave it off; the merging of model-proposed relationships into reads with evidence 'model'; the status line when no CLI provider is available.

hldContextSlice.rolloutPhase: Phase A — a daemon that stays up and reads that tell the truth

nonFunctional.performance: Reading one file's entities costs in proportion to that file's rows, and one repository's in proportion to that repository's rows. A file commit is one write transaction whose size is bounded by one file. A first full index holds more pending rows than today until the cross-file pass runs, and that pass does more work; this is accepted under the accuracy rule. Index jobs take precedence in the queue and a derived pass yields between its units of work, so a commit waits for at most one unit of a pass. Model calls are serial; the mid-tier pass sends only new or changed documents. Vector writes keep the plain insert for entities first stored in the same commit, so a first full index writes vectors at today's cost; the upsert, which costs more against a large vector table, is used only for changed entities and for the backfill, and Story s2's design measures it on this repository.
nonFunctional.security: No store is opened outside the daemon and no model is reached except through the local provider or the CLI providers. The ignore-file proposal sends the model file names and manifest names, not file contents, and writes into the user's repository only when no root ignore file exists. Document text sent to the mid-tier model goes through the user's own CLI session, as other mid-tier calls do.
nonFunctional.observability: Repository status carries the completeness counts and the reason a repository is incomplete. A relationship the store refuses is logged at warn with its reason and counted, not logged at debug. A fallback ignore file, a skipped language reader, a store failure after its locks were taken away, and a model-proposed capability that is off each state their cause where status is read. Each derived row carries the generation it was computed from.
nonFunctional.durability: The file commit is atomic in LMDB: after a crash a file holds its old rows or its new rows. Vectors are written after the commit and may be missing after a crash; the gap is recorded by an empty embedding marker, checked against the vector table on open, and backfilled, and the repository reads as incomplete until it is, unless the embedding backend is unavailable, which is reported as its own reason. The IndexState fields that the tables can answer are recounted when the store is opened; the rest, including the paths of files that could not be committed, are persisted in the state row and survive a restart. Every new table and value arrives by a migration step applied on open; no existing key or kind byte changes, so an older store is brought forward without a re-index. Derived tables can be dropped and recomputed without loss.

api.name: getGraphStore

returns.meaning: The one open store of this process, opened on first call, as today.

errors.type: LmdbStoreNotOwnerError (new, a subclass of the store's existing LmdbStoreError)
errors.condition: The path to open is the live path (PATHS.lmdb) and this process has not declared itself the store's owner. The message names the path, says that only the daemon may open the live store, and tells a test to set a temporary path with setGraphStorePath.

The store's health record is locks-lost. Every read and write in the code begins with getGraphStore, so this is the one read-side place the failure is raised; no single wrapper for reads exists (modules take the handle and call the library on a sub-database directly).
As today: a failed open, a schema version newer than the code, a failed migration.

preconditions: For the live path only: the process has called one of the two new declarations before the first open. The daemon's entry point (src/daemon/index.ts) declares itself the owner. The MCP server's entry point declares itself a permitted reader: a temporary allowance, because the analyze step runs in that process today and reads the store directly (src/mcp/server.ts:402; 35 files under src/analyze import the store layer). Story s11 moves that work into the daemon and removes the allowance and its declaration.
For any other path (a test's temporary store set through setGraphStorePath): none, as today.
postconditions: A process that has made neither declaration never holds a descriptor on the live store or its lock file: the check runs before the library's open is called. Until Story s11 lands, the MCP server's process is the one exception, and acceptance criterion ac1 is met for every other process; it is met in full when s11 removes the allowance.
The check compares resolved paths, so a relative path or a symbolic link to the live store is refused as well.

A lock failure first met on a read through a handle a module already holds is not caught at that read; it is recorded by the next write or raised by the next getGraphStore call, whichever comes first.

One more process opens the live store today and is not let in: the CLI's own process, through its in-process review of an artifact (src/cli/services/workflow.ts calls reviewArtifactFile, whose probe calls resolveSourceRoots in src/workflow/review/source-roots.ts with no injected reader, which reads the repository's entities through the store). That read swallows every failure by contract and falls back to the repository root, so a refusal there would degrade the CLI's review silently. It is given an injected reader that asks the daemon (see the data model, 'source-root reader for a review outside the daemon'), and the fallback, when it is taken, is stated in the review's output. The search for openers behind this design covered direct imports of the store layer; before the refusal is switched on it is repeated over everything the CLI's and the MCP server's entry points import, and any further opener found is handled the same way or raised.

api.name: setGraphStorePath

parameters.name: path
parameters.purpose: The store path for this process, in place of the live default.

preconditions: Called before the first getGraphStore, as today.
postconditions: Unchanged in behaviour. It is now the way a test, and only a test, gets a store without declaring ownership: any path that is not the live one stays open to any process.

The two test files that reach the live store today (src/analyze/explore/__tests__/freeform-probe-scope.test.ts and phase5-explorations-params.test.ts) call it with a temporary directory, as the 80 other store-using test files do.

api.name: closeGraphStore

returns.meaning: Resolves when the store is closed or when the close has been skipped.

postconditions: When the store's health record says 'locks-lost', the library's close is not called: it hangs for ever once the semaphores are gone. The function forgets its handle, logs that the close was skipped and why, and resolves.

api.name: stopDaemon

returns.type: Promise<StopOutcome>, where StopOutcome = { stopped: true; forced: boolean; pid?: number }
returns.meaning: How the daemon stopped: by itself (forced false) or by a forced kill after the wait (forced true, with the pid that was killed).

errors.condition: No socket and no live daemon pid, as today: the shutdown request rejects before any wait. Unchanged; a stop of a stopped daemon stays an error and the CLI's two callers (src/cli/command.ts and the daemon pane) print it as they do now.

Only when the forced kill itself fails (the process is still alive after it, or the pid file names a process this user cannot signal). The message names the pid and says what was tried. The present 'daemon did not stop within 30 s' is no longer a final outcome.
The pid in the pid file is alive but its command line is not a daemon's. The message names the pid and the command line; the pid file and the socket are left in place.

postconditions: Sends the daemon.shutdown request with a bound of 5 seconds on the reply: the request client has no time-out today, and a daemon whose main thread is blocked while its socket still listens accepts the connection and never answers, so an unbounded await would never reach the wait or the kill. On a reply, a refused connection with a live daemon pid, or the bound passing, it waits through waitForStop as today. If the wait ends without a stop it sends SIGKILL to the pid in the pid file, waits for the process to be gone, removes the pid file and the socket file, and returns forced true.

The pid is checked to be a daemon process before it is killed: its command line must end in the daemon's entry file (the path suffix daemon/index.js). The check does not compare against DAEMON_ENTRY as exported by src/cli/services/daemon.ts, because that is the entry of the CLI's own checkout, while the control script starts the daemon from the installed one ($HOME/.insrc/daemon or INSRC_DAEMON_ROOT), so a CLI run from a development checkout would not match a live installed daemon. When the pid is alive and its command line does not match, nothing is killed and nothing is removed: the stop fails with an error naming the pid and its command line, since removing the pid file and socket of a live daemon would let a second one start on the same store.
restart (src/cli/services/maintenance.ts) reports a forced stop in its log lines and goes on to start.

The signature change reaches the service type at src/cli/services/index.ts (stopDaemon(): Promise<void> today) and the three callers: src/cli/command.ts, src/cli/panes/DaemonPane.tsx and restart in src/cli/services/maintenance.ts.

api.name: restart

returns.meaning: As today; the steps list gains 'force-stop' when the stop was forced.

postconditions: A daemon that did not stop by itself no longer ends the restart with an error and a daemon left half down: the stop is forced, the fact is logged through onLog, and the start follows.

scripts/daemon-ctl.sh behaves the same way, through one shell function used at both places where the script stops a daemon and gives up today: cmd_stop, and the stale-daemon branch of cmd_start ('stale daemon did not shut down within 30 s'). After wait_for_daemon_stop fails, the function checks that the pid's command line (ps -o command= -p "$pid") ends in daemon/index.js, the same rule as the CLI's; on a match it sends SIGKILL, waits for the process to be gone, removes the pid file and the socket, and logs 'daemon did not stop within 30 s; killed (pid N)'; it dies only if the process survives the kill. A live pid whose command line does not match is not killed and its pid file is not removed; the script dies naming the pid and the command line.

dataModelChanges.details: Two module-level flags, false by default, each set by one new exported function that takes no argument and can only set it: an owner declaration, called by the daemon's entry point before anything opens the store, and a permitted-reader declaration, called by the MCP server's entry point. They are deliberately not environment variables and not read from a file: child processes inherit neither a call nor a module variable, so a test run or a CLI provider started by the daemon is neither. getGraphStore reads them only when the resolved path equals the live path. The permitted-reader declaration is temporary: it exists because the MCP server runs the analyze step in its own process today, and Story s11 removes the function and its one call when that work has moved into the daemon. It is named so that a search for it finds exactly what s11 must delete.

The one record of whether this process's store can still be used. It starts as ok, is set once, and never returns to ok in the same process; only a restart clears it. How the failure shows itself was measured on 2026-10-11 by breaking a temporary store's locks and then using it, and the three kinds of call behave differently: a read (a get) throws at once with the library's code -30775 (MDB_LOCK_FAILURE); a synchronous transaction throws at once with code 22 ('Invalid argument'), not -30775; and an asynchronous transaction, which is what withWriteTxn uses and most writes go through, never settles: it neither resolves nor rejects, and a synchronous transaction attempted after it hung. Detection is therefore in three places. (1) withWriteTxnSync catches an error with either code. Code 22 is the general 'Invalid argument' and the record cannot be cleared without a restart, so before recording it confirms with the same probe read as below: only if the probe throws -30775 is locks-lost recorded; otherwise the original error is rethrown unchanged. (2) withWriteTxn bounds its wait: when an asynchronous transaction has not settled within a fixed time (10 seconds; an ordinary write here takes milliseconds) it probes the store with one read of a fixed key. If the probe throws -30775 the record becomes locks-lost and the wrapper rejects; if the probe returns, the write is only slow and the wrapper goes on waiting. The probe is a read because a read is the one call measured to fail fast and cleanly in this state. (3) Reads have no wrapper (modules take the handle and call the library on a sub-database directly), so a -30775 thrown by a read surfaces in the caller. The daemon's request server has three catch sites (the standard request, the standard handler reached through a stream request, and the stream handler, all in src/daemon/server.ts) and its queue has one (the job runner in src/daemon/queue.ts); each reduces an error to its message today, and each reads the error's code first, records locks-lost for -30775 and answers with the named error. A read that fails outside those four sites (a timer, the boot sequence) or inside a handler that swallows its own failures (the review's source-root read does) is not recorded there. Two things cover it: the daemon's periodic reader check, which already runs every five minutes, also makes the probe read and records a failure; and the next write records it through its bound. A failure can therefore go unrecorded for up to that interval, which is accepted. In every case the error raised to the caller is LmdbStoreLocksLostError, whose message states the true cause (the store's locks were removed by another process that opened and closed it after this process lost its file lock on the lock file) and does not repeat the library's advice about a system limit; the library's own text is kept in the record for the log. Once the record is locks-lost, getGraphStore throws the named error to every caller, so no later call reaches the library. The record is read by the daemon's status, by getGraphStore, by closeGraphStore and by the shutdown.

One optional field carrying the store's health, absent when it is ok so that today's consumers see no change. The daemon.status request fills it from getStoreHealth. The request reads the repository list from the store first, outside any guard today (`repos: await listRepos(db)` in src/daemon/index.ts), and by this design that read throws once the store has failed; the handler therefore guards it and, on a store failure, returns the status with an empty repository list and storeFailure set, which is the one moment the field is needed. The CLI's daemon pane and both editor plugins show the cause line when it is present; the mirrored type in the plugins gains the same optional field.

Today both ends of the shutdown call process.exit, which runs the library's exit hook; with the locks lost that hook never returns, on the main thread, so the 20-second backstop timer cannot fire either. A third call exists outside the shutdown: reportFatal, registered for uncaught exceptions and unhandled rejections, ends with process.exit after 50 milliseconds, and a rejection with the new named error that nothing awaits would reach it. New invariant: once StoreHealth is locks-lost the daemon never calls process.exit, at any of the three places. When a stop is asked for with the store failed, the shutdown does not wait for the queue to drain, since a job held in a store call would never finish: directly from the shutdown function it stops the queue, the watcher and the server, skips the store's close, removes the pid file and the socket file, writes its last log line synchronously to the daemon's log file, and ends the process with SIGKILL to itself, which runs no exit hook. reportFatal does the same when the store has failed: it already writes its line synchronously, and it then removes the pid file and the socket and ends by SIGKILL in place of process.exit. With StoreHealth ok all three are unchanged. A hang that the daemon did not foresee is ended by the control paths (stopDaemon and scripts/daemon-ctl.sh).

dataModelChanges.entity: lock-file open diagnostic (new, in the daemon)
dataModelChanges.details: What in the daemon closes a second descriptor on the lock file is not identified. So that the next occurrence names it, the daemon wraps, at start-up, the functions of Node's fs module and of fs/promises that open a file by path (open, openSync, readFile, readFileSync, copyFile, copyFileSync, cp, cpSync, createReadStream and the promise forms of open, readFile, copyFile and cp), and re-syncs the built-in module's exports so that code which imported them by name sees the wrap. For a path that resolves to the live store's lock file or data file the wrap logs the call stack at warn, once per distinct stack, and lets the call proceed. It is a diagnostic and is best effort: a route into the file system that goes around these functions is not seen, and its test opens the lock file through fs.promises.readFile, the route the daemon's own tools use. The daemon's file tools also refuse the store's two files by path, with a named error, since reading them is never useful and is the one known way to drop the lock. The refusal is one small check function, called with the path after symbolic links are resolved (the tools' shared helper resolves a path without following links, which is not enough). It is called from the shared path helper of the file tools (resolvePath in src/daemon/tools/builtins/file/helpers.ts) and, because the copy and move tools resolve their two paths themselves and never call that helper when they run, also from the execute step and the approval gate of copy and move, for both the source and the target, and from the search tools' own path handling. Every tool is thereby covered: read, edit, multi-edit, copy, delete, write and move among the file tools, and grep, glob, list-dir and recent among the search tools. Its test calls each tool's own execute, not the helper. Of these, read, edit, multi-edit, copy, delete and grep read a file's content in the daemon's process today.

dataModelChanges.entity: source-root reader for a review outside the daemon (new option and new daemon request)
dataModelChanges.details: The CLI's in-process review cannot be handed a reader today: the chain from the CLI is reviewArtifactFile (src/workflow/review/run-artifact.ts), review (src/workflow/review/review.ts), gatherEvidence (src/workflow/review/probe.ts) and resolveSourceRoots (src/workflow/review/source-roots.ts), and only the last takes a reader. One optional field, the reader, is added to the options of the first three and passed down. It is optional, so the daemon's own review (src/daemon/workflow-review-rpc.ts) and the MCP server's review step keep the default reader and are unchanged. The CLI (src/cli/services/workflow.ts) passes a reader that calls one new read-only daemon request, which takes a repository path and returns what the default reader returns: that repository's entities as resolveSourceRoots needs them. When the request fails the review falls back to the repository root, as it does today on any read failure, and its output now says that it did and why.

errorCases.scenario: A process that is neither the daemon nor, until Story s11, the MCP server reaches for the live store: a test that set no temporary path, a script, or new code in the CLI.
errorCases.detection: getGraphStore compares the resolved path it is about to open with the resolved live path and finds neither declaration made, before the library's open is called.
errorCases.response: Throws LmdbStoreNotOwnerError naming the path and the remedy (a temporary path for a test; a daemon request for anything else). No descriptor on the store or its lock file is ever opened.
errorCases.userImpact: The offending test or tool fails at once with a clear message. The daemon is unaffected.

errorCases.scenario: The store's locks are taken away while the daemon runs (the failure of the issue), by a route this Story did not close.
errorCases.detection: Three ways, by what was measured: a synchronous transaction throws with code 22 or -30775 and withWriteTxnSync catches it; an asynchronous transaction does not settle, and withWriteTxn, after 10 seconds, probes the store with a read that throws -30775; a read throws -30775 into its caller, and the daemon's request dispatcher or queue runner catches it.
errorCases.response: StoreHealth becomes locks-lost with the time, the operation and how it was detected; the named error LmdbStoreLocksLostError is raised with the true cause; the daemon logs it once at error with the library's own text beside it. From then on getGraphStore throws the same named error, so later calls fail fast without reaching the library. The daemon keeps serving what does not need the store (status, shutdown).
errorCases.userImpact: Requests that need the store fail with a message that says the store's locks were removed by another process and that the daemon must be restarted. Status shows the same line.

errorCases.scenario: The daemon's status is asked for after the store has failed.
errorCases.detection: The status handler's read of the repository list throws LmdbStoreLocksLostError, raised by getGraphStore.
errorCases.response: The handler catches it, returns the status with an empty repository list and with storeFailure filled from the health record, and does not throw.
errorCases.userImpact: Status still answers and says why the store is unusable.

errorCases.scenario: The daemon is asked to stop after its store has failed.
errorCases.detection: The shutdown reads StoreHealth and finds locks-lost.
errorCases.response: Without waiting for the queue to drain, it stops the queue, the watcher and the server, skips the store's close, removes the pid file and the socket file, writes a last line to the daemon's log synchronously, and sends itself SIGKILL. process.exit is not called, because the library's exit hook would hang.
errorCases.userImpact: The daemon is gone within its normal stop time and a start works with no manual clean-up. In-flight queue work is abandoned, as it would be on any kill; the next start resumes from the stored state.

errorCases.scenario: The daemon hangs during a stop for a reason it did not record (the store's close hangs although StoreHealth is ok, or any other hang on the main thread).
errorCases.detection: stopDaemon's wait, or the control script's wait_for_daemon_stop, ends with the pid still alive.
errorCases.response: The control path checks that the pid is a daemon process, sends SIGKILL, waits for it to be gone, removes the pid file and the socket file, and reports a forced stop with the pid.
errorCases.userImpact: The stop takes the full wait (30 s) and then succeeds; the message says the daemon was killed. A restart goes on to start.

errorCases.scenario: The daemon cannot answer: its socket is gone while its process is alive (the state the issue found), or its main thread is blocked and it accepts the connection but never replies.
errorCases.detection: stopDaemon's shutdown request fails with a connection error, or gets no reply within 5 seconds, while the pid in the pid file is alive.
errorCases.response: It does not treat the failed request as 'already stopped': it goes straight to the wait and the forced kill.
errorCases.userImpact: The half-down daemon is cleared by an ordinary stop or restart.

errorCases.scenario: The forced kill fails: the process survives SIGKILL, or the pid belongs to another user.
errorCases.detection: The pid is still alive after the kill and a short wait, or the kill call returns a permission error.
errorCases.response: The control path throws or dies with a message naming the pid and what was tried, and leaves the pid file in place so that a start still refuses to run a second daemon.
errorCases.userImpact: The user is told exactly which process to deal with.

errorCases.scenario: Something in the daemon opens the store's lock file.
errorCases.detection: The wrapped file-open functions see a path that resolves to the live lock file.
errorCases.response: The open proceeds unchanged and its call stack is logged at warn, once per distinct stack. The daemon's own file tools refuse the path with a named error before any open.
errorCases.userImpact: None at the time. The log names the code to fix, which is the part of the cause that is still unknown.

errorCases.scenario: A write is slow but the store is healthy (a large transaction, a busy disk).
errorCases.detection: withWriteTxn's 10-second bound passes and its probe read returns normally.
errorCases.response: Nothing is recorded; the wrapper goes on waiting for the write and probes again at the same interval.

errorCases.scenario: The pid file names a live process whose command line is not a daemon's.
errorCases.detection: The command-line check before the forced kill fails for a pid that is alive.
errorCases.response: Nothing is killed and nothing is removed; the stop fails with the pid and its command line in the message.
errorCases.userImpact: The user sees which process holds the pid and decides; no second daemon can start on the same store.

errorCases.scenario: An error escapes every handler after the store has failed (an unhandled rejection or an uncaught exception).
errorCases.detection: reportFatal runs and reads StoreHealth as locks-lost.
errorCases.response: It writes its line synchronously, removes the pid file and the socket, and ends the process by SIGKILL to itself; it does not call process.exit.
errorCases.userImpact: The daemon is gone and can be started again, where it would otherwise hang with its pid file in place.

invariantsToPreserve.text: A test that sets a temporary store path keeps working with no other change: 80 test files do so today and none of them declares ownership.
getGraphStore returns one store per process and opens it lazily on first call; closeGraphStore closes it. Neither signature changes.
A healthy daemon's shutdown is unchanged: it drains the queue, closes its connections in the same order, clears the pid file and exits, with the same 20-second backstop.
The daemon's status request never throws and its existing fields keep their meaning; the new field is optional and absent when the store is healthy.
A stop of a daemon that stops by itself reports and behaves as today; the forced kill happens only after the existing wait has ended without a stop.
A client session's step tools keep working throughout this Story: the MCP server's process is not refused the store until Story s11 has moved its reads into the daemon.

migration.stateBefore: Per the s1 bundle on the store and the stop, and the direct reads recorded with it: getGraphStore opens whatever path is set, and the path defaults to the live store, so any process that imports the store layer opens the live store; the MCP server does so for every analyze step, which runs in its own process and reads the store directly for scope resolution, the last-indexed time, every lookup and the cache, and two test files do so because they set no temporary path. Nothing in src handles the library's lock failure: it reaches the log as the library's text about a system limit. The daemon's shutdown ends in process.exit on both of its paths, and stopDaemon and the control script give up after 30 seconds with the daemon left half down. DaemonStatus has no field for a store failure.
migration.stateAfter: The live store opens only in a process that has declared itself its owner (the daemon) or, until Story s11, a permitted reader (the MCP server); every other process is refused before any file is opened. A lock failure is recorded once as locks-lost with its true cause, raised as a named error by the write wrappers and by getGraphStore, and shown in the daemon's status, whose handler answers even when the store has failed. A daemon whose store has failed ends itself without calling process.exit; a stop that overruns is finished by a forced kill from stopDaemon or from the control script's stop and start, which clean the pid file and the socket and say what they did. Any open of the store's lock file inside the daemon is logged with its call stack. Story s11 then moves the step tools into the daemon and removes the permitted-reader declaration, which completes acceptance criterion ac1.

migrationSteps.action: Add the health record and the two named errors, with detection at the three measured places: the synchronous write wrapper (codes 22 and -30775), the asynchronous write wrapper's bounded wait and read probe, the three catch sites of the daemon's request server and the queue's job runner for a failing read, and the probe in the periodic reader check. Add the optional storeFailure field to the daemon's status and its mirrored types; the status handler guards its read of the repository list. Nothing else reads the record yet.

Change the stop paths: stopDaemon bounds its shutdown request, returns an outcome and forces the stop after its wait, killing only a pid whose command line ends in daemon/index.js; restart reports a forced stop and goes on; the control script gets one forced-stop function used by its stop and by the stale-daemon branch of its start. Independent of every other step, and useful by itself against the hang as it occurs today.

Change the daemon's shutdown, closeGraphStore and getGraphStore to read the health record: getGraphStore throws the named error once the store has failed, and the shutdown and the close skip the store's close and end by a kill signal to itself when the record is locks-lost. Requires step 1. The shutdown does not wait for the queue when the store has failed, and reportFatal ends the same way.

Give the two test files that reach the live store a temporary one, and thread the optional reader through the three review functions, add the read-only daemon request, and have the CLI's review pass a reader that calls it, with its fallback stated in the review's output. Repeat the search for openers over everything the CLI's and the MCP server's entry points import.

Add the two declarations, call the owner one from the daemon's entry point and the permitted-reader one from the MCP server's entry point, and switch on the refusal in getGraphStore. This is the step that can break a caller, so it comes after the two test files have been moved; the full test sweep is run with it before it is committed, and any test it newly fails is a test that was opening the live store.

Add the lock-file open diagnostic in the daemon and the refusal of the store's two files, called from the file tools' shared path helper, from the copy and move tools themselves, and from the search tools.

Deploy: update the installed daemon, then restart client sessions so that their MCP server processes run the new code. Run the smoke checks (an outside script is refused; a restart of a healthy daemon behaves as before; an analysis from a client session still works).

Hand-over to Story s11: when s11 has moved the step tools into the daemon it deletes the permitted-reader declaration and its call, after which the MCP server's process is refused like any other. Not part of this Story's delivery.

migration.backwardCompat: No stored data changes and no migration of the store is involved. DaemonStatus gains one optional field, absent when the store is healthy, so a consumer that does not know it is unaffected. stopDaemon's return changes from nothing to an outcome object and it no longer rejects on a time-out, though it still rejects when no daemon is running; its service type and its three callers in the CLI are updated in the same change. MaintenanceResult's steps list may contain a new value, 'force-stop'. The control script's stop now exits 0 after a forced kill where it exited 4. The one behaviour that can break an existing caller is the refusal of the live store to a process that is not the daemon: by design it breaks any test or script that opened the live store without setting a temporary path. The MCP server's process keeps its access through the temporary declaration until Story s11, so client sessions are unaffected by this Story.

alternativesConsidered.name: An explicit owner declaration in the store, a recorded store health, and a stop that ends from outside the main thread
alternativesConsidered.oneLineSummary: The daemon declares itself the store's owner before it opens it; the store refuses the live path to anyone else; a store failure is recorded once and read by status and by shutdown; the stop is finished by a forced kill, from the daemon itself when it knows the store has failed and from the control paths otherwise.
alternativesConsidered.approach:
The store module gains an explicit declaration of who may open the live path. The daemon's entry point makes it before its first open; the store's open checks it whenever the path is the live one and throws a named error otherwise, so a temporary path set by a test stays open to anyone. The MCP server's process, which runs the analyze step itself and reads the store directly, is let in by a second, temporary declaration until Story s11 has moved that work into the daemon; the two test files that reach the live store get a temporary one. A store failure is recorded in one place: the store's write wrapper recognises the library's lock failure, records it with a true description of the cause, and raises a named error in place of the library's text. The daemon's status reads that record.

Stopping uses the same record. The library's exit hook hangs on the main thread once the store's semaphores are gone, so no timer in the daemon can end it. When the record says the store has failed, the shutdown skips the store's close, clears the pid file and the socket, and ends the process with a kill signal to itself, which runs no exit hook. For a hang that was not foreseen, the two control paths (the control script and the CLI's stop) escalate after their wait to a forced kill of the recorded pid, remove the pid file and the socket, and say that they did so.
pros: The refusal is decided by a call the daemon makes on purpose, so it cannot be satisfied by accident: a test or a tool that imports the store and forgets a temporary path fails at once with a named error, in place of breaking the daemon hours later.
It removes the second ingredient of the failure (another process closing the live store) without needing to know which daemon code drops the lock, which is not yet identified.
One record of store health serves the three acceptance criteria: the write after another process's attempt (ac1), the stop (ac2) and the status (ac3).
The self-kill and the control-path escalation cover the two cases separately: a failure the daemon has seen, and a hang it has not.
cons: Ending the process with a kill signal skips every exit hook, the logger's flush included, so the last log lines must be written synchronously before it.
The declaration is one more thing a new entry point that legitimately owns a store would have to call; today there is one such entry point.

Until Story s11 lands, one other process (the MCP server) still opens and closes the live store, so the original failure stays possible through it; this Story bounds the damage (the daemon reports the failure and stops cleanly) but does not yet remove that route.

alternativesConsidered.name: Ownership inferred from the pid file, and a watchdog thread that bounds the exit
alternativesConsidered.oneLineSummary: The store allows the live path only to the process whose pid is in the daemon's pid file; a worker thread in the daemon kills the process if the shutdown overruns.
alternativesConsidered.approach:
No declaration is added. The store's open compares its own pid with the daemon's pid file and refuses the live path when they differ. The MCP server's cache access and the two tests are moved as in the first alternative. A store failure is recognised in the write wrapper and recorded for status.

The stop is bounded inside the daemon by a second thread: when shutdown begins, a worker thread starts a timer and sends the process a kill signal when it expires, whatever the main thread is doing. The control paths are left as they are.
pros: No new call for the daemon's entry point; the rule follows from a file that already exists.
The watchdog bounds every shutdown, foreseen or not, from inside the daemon, so the control script and the CLI need no change.
cons: The pid file is written after the store is first opened in the daemon's start-up, so the check would refuse the daemon itself unless the order of start-up is changed, and a stale pid file from a crashed daemon would refuse the next one.
A process can match by accident: a test that writes a pid file in a temporary home, or pid reuse after a crash.

A worker thread that exists only to kill the process is a second mechanism to keep alive and to test, and a hang with the pid file already cleared leaves the control paths saying the daemon stopped when the watchdog has not yet fired.
alternativesConsidered.reasonRejected: Bounds the stop well, but the ownership test rests on a file that is written after the store opens and can be stale or matched by accident.

alternativesConsidered.name: A launcher-set environment marker, with the stop bounded only by the control paths
alternativesConsidered.oneLineSummary: The control script sets an environment variable that marks the daemon; the store refuses the live path without it; nothing changes in the daemon's shutdown, and the control paths kill after their wait.
alternativesConsidered.approach:
The script and the CLI's start set a variable in the daemon's environment, and the store's open requires it for the live path. The MCP server's cache access and the two tests are moved as in the first alternative. The library's lock failure is recognised in the write wrapper and recorded for status.

The daemon's shutdown is not changed. When it hangs, the control script and the CLI's stop wait their 30 seconds, then kill the recorded pid and clean up.
pros: The smallest change inside the daemon: no declaration call and no change to the shutdown sequence.
The escalation in the control paths is needed in any case and is the whole of the stop work here.
cons: Child processes inherit the environment: every process the daemon spawns (the CLI providers, test runs started by a build) would carry the marker and be allowed the live store, which is the very case to exclude.
A daemon whose store has failed takes the full wait to stop every time, although it knows at once that its close will hang; the criterion asks for its normal stop time.
A daemon started by hand without the marker cannot open its own store.
alternativesConsidered.reasonRejected: The marker is inherited by every process the daemon spawns, which lets in exactly the processes the rule is meant to keep out, and a failed daemon always takes the full wait to stop.

feedback.author: Subho Ghosh
feedback.comment: Revised 2026-10-11 after the first daemon review (block: 2 HIGH, 3 MED) and the stakeholder's decision to run the step tools inside the daemon (Story s11). (1) The analyze step runs in the MCP server's process and reads the live store directly, far beyond its cache; the cache move is taken out of this Story and the whole move belongs to s11. Until s11 lands the MCP server is let in by a temporary permitted-reader declaration, which s11 deletes; acceptance criterion ac1 is met in full only then. (2) The status handler guards its store read so that it answers after a store failure. (3) Reads have no wrapper; getGraphStore raises the failure. (4) A stop of a stopped daemon stays an error, as today. (5) The control script's start shares the forced-stop function with its stop. The pid check reuses DAEMON_ENTRY.

feedback.author: Subho Ghosh
feedback.comment: Revised twice more on 2026-10-11, after the second and third daemon reviews (blocks of 5 and 4). Detection now follows a measurement of the failed store: a read throws -30775, a synchronous transaction throws 22, an asynchronous transaction never settles; so the asynchronous wrapper bounds its wait and probes with a read, the synchronous wrapper confirms code 22 with the same probe, the request server and queue catch a failing read, and the periodic reader check probes too. Also: the CLI review reaches source roots through a daemon request; stopDaemon bounds its request and never removes the pid file of a live non-matching process; the refusal of the store files is called from the copy and move tools themselves; reportFatal and a stop with the store failed end by self-kill without waiting for the queue. The third round's fixes are NOT re-reviewed.

feedback.author: Claude (builder)
feedback.comment: Correction found while building Task t3 on 2026-10-11 (src/db/graph/__tests__/lock-loss-reproduction.test.ts). This design says a read on a store whose locks were removed throws code -30775. That holds only for a process that has never read from the store. A process that has read before, which the daemon always has because the store module reads while opening, fails a read with code 22 and a message containing MDB_BAD_RSLOT ("Invalid reuse of reader locktable slot: The reader lock pid 0 ... does not match env pid"). The earlier measurement used a process that had not read. Consequence for Tasks t4 and t5: wherever this design says a read or probe "throws -30775", the rule is "throws -30775, or throws code 22 with MDB_BAD_RSLOT in its message". A bare code 22 from a synchronous transaction is still only confirmed by the probe read. The asynchronous and synchronous write behaviours are as designed.
